UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                   )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                        )                Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                   )

                            MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE ANSWER,
                                    AND ANSWER, OF
                         EAST KENTUCKY POWER COOPERATIVE, INC.

           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 East

Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc. (“EKPC”) moves for leave to file this answer and answers the

September 23, 2026 answer submitted by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) in the above-

captioned proceeding.2 EKPC’s Protest in this proceeding opposed PJM’s proposed revisions to its

Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load

Serving Entities in the PJM Region (“RAA”) to establish an Interim Resource Adequacy Service

(“IRAS”). As explained in EKPC’s Protest, certain provisions of PJM’s IRAS Proposal are unjust

and unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, and inconsistent with the Commission’s cost-causation

principles.3 PJM’s Answer does not cure those defects. It largely responds to arguments EKPC did

not make or answers EKPC’s concerns only at a level of generality that avoids the implementation

problems identified in EKPC’s Protest and the Affidavit of Marc D. Montalvo (“Montalvo

Affidavit”). For the reasons set forth herein and in EKPC’s Protest, the Commission should reject

or require revisions to those elements of the IRAS Proposal that would impose IRAS exposure,

compensation costs, or curtailment risk on loads and Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”) that did not


1
    See 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2026).
2
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., “Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.,” Docket
No. ER26-3515-000 (filed Sept. 23, 2026) (“PJM Answer”).
3
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., “Limited Protest of East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc.,” Docket No. ER26-3515-
000 (filed Sept. 3, 2026) (“EKPC Protest”).
 cause the asserted resource adequacy deficiency or that have already supported their load through

a prudent resource portfolio.

        I.       MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE ANSWER

        Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure generally prohibits

answers to answers or protests unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority. Good cause

exists to accept this Answer because PJM’s Answer misconstrues EKPC’s portfolio-sufficiency,

resource-attribution, and transferability arguments and does not resolve the real-time curtailment

and compensation issues identified in EKPC’s Protest and supporting affidavits. This Answer will

assist the Commission in its decision-making process4 and clarify the record.5 For these reasons,

the Commission should accept this Answer.

        II.      ANSWER

                 A.       PJM Failed to Address or Misstates Significant Concerns Raised in
                          EKPC’s Protest.

        In its Protest, EKPC explained that a legitimate reliability objective does not justify the

Commission’s acceptance of a proposal that has not been shown in its entirety to be just and

reasonable, that is potentially unduly discriminatory, and that is inconsistent with the

Commission’s cost-causation framework. EKPC’s Protest raised several concerns regarding

aspects of the IRAS Proposal, and PJM’s Answer misconstrues or does not address the central

issues raised by EKPC.



4
 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,110, P 22 (2024) (accepting answers to protests and answers
because they assisted the Commission in its decision-making process); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 181 FERC ¶
61,162, P 29 (2022) (same).
5
  See, e.g., Potomac-Appalachian Transmission Highline, LLC, 140 FERC ¶ 61,229, P 102 (2012) (accepting answer
to an answer because it provided material evidence that corrected the record and informed the Commission’s decision-
making process); High Island Offshore Sys., L.L.C., 113 FERC ¶ 61,202, P 8 (2005) (accepting an answer to a protest
because it assisted the Commission with a more complete record); N.E. Utils. Servs. Co. v. NRG Energy, Inc., 101
FERC ¶ 61,327, P 17 (2002) (accepting answer to an answer because it helped clarify issues in the proceeding).



                                                         2
        The defects warrant different forms of relief. The Commission should reject the

compensation provision and any interpretation of an IRAS Action that would permit curtailment

of non-IRAS load because those provisions lack an adequate record basis and exceed the stated

scope of IRAS. Additionally, the Commission should condition acceptance on tariff revisions

establishing a portfolio-sufficiency pathway, interim recognition of operating resources pending

their first available RPM commitment, reasonable reassignment of unused Bring Your Own New

Capacity (“BYONC”) UCAP MW, and a Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”) exemption tied to

a sufficient FRR Capacity Plan.

       PJM Must Recognize the Value of an LSE’s Existing Portfolio. PJM’s Answer discusses

flexibility within the BYONC construct, but it does not answer EKPC’s separate portfolio-

sufficiency argument. PJM repeatedly states that the PJM Region needs new capacity, but that

regional observation does not establish that every New Large Load served by every RPM-

participating LSE lacks capacity support or contributes to the resource adequacy shortfall IRAS is

intended to address. EKPC’s point is not that existing capacity should be “repackaged” as BYONC.

Rather, a self-supply LSE that demonstrates, using PJM-validated UCAP values and Large Load

included in the Registry and verified to be online in the relevant Delivery Year, that its portfolio is

sufficient to serve its aggregate obligations, including incremental load growth, should not be

treated as though its load is unsupported merely because PJM’s proposed eligibility rules recognize

only BYONC (including BYONC tied to specific loads that ultimately may not need all allocated

BYONC) or Allocated RBP UCAP MW. Curtailing portfolio-supported load also breaks the causal

link on which PJM relies to justify IRAS because PJM has not shown that an LSE making that

demonstration causes the deficiency IRAS purports to remedy. The Commission therefore should




                                                  3
 require PJM to establish a portfolio-sufficiency pathway with objective eligibility, verification, and

anti-double-counting requirements.

           RPM Auction Timing Disconnect for BYONC Qualification. PJM does not explain why

a resource that is online, not committed outside PJM, capable of providing energy and ancillary

services, and expected to be offered into RPM at the first available opportunity should provide no

IRAS offset during the period between commercial operation and its first available RPM

commitment. EKPC does not object to requiring a resource that offsets IRAS exposure to assume

obligations comparable to those of an Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”)-committed Capacity

Resource. But making prior RPM commitment an absolute prerequisite goes further than necessary

and can leave load exposed to curtailment after the underlying reliability concern has been

addressed by an operating resource. The Liberty RICE and Cooper CCGT examples demonstrate

that commercial-operation dates follow permitting, construction, testing, and interconnection

schedules—not the June 1 Delivery Year boundary—and that an operating resource may support

reliability for months before it clears an RPM auction.6 PJM’s filing therefore treats resources with

comparable present reliability capability differently based solely on administrative timing. The

Commission should require PJM to recognize an operating resource pending its first available

RPM commitment where the resource: (1) has achieved commercial operation; (2) has PJM-

confirmed deliverability and a PJM-determined accredited UCAP capability; (3) is not committed

outside PJM or counted toward another obligation; (4) is subject to PJM dispatch, outage-

reporting, testing, and performance requirements; and (5) is bound to offer into the first RPM

Auction for which it is eligible.




6
    EKPC Protest at 19. See also Montalvo Affidavit at PP 26-27 and Tucker Affidavit at PP 13-16.



                                                          4
            Committing Specific Capacity Resources to Specific Loads. PJM’s response answers a

different question than the question raised by EKPC. EKPC did not argue that BYONC must be

electrically deliverable to or physically serve a particular New Large Load.7 EKPC’s concern is

that IRAS exposure turns on whether PJM recognizes specific UCAP MW as assigned to a specific

New Large Load, rather than whether the serving LSE’s aggregate portfolio is sufficient to satisfy

its aggregate load and reliability obligations. That remains resource-to-load attribution, even if

PJM does not require the identified resource to physically serve the customer.8 Resource adequacy

studies, integrated resource plans, reserve-margin analyses, and RPM obligations ordinarily test

portfolios against aggregate load; they do not require permanent assignments between individual

resources and individual retail customers. PJM has not explained why that portfolio-based

paradigm suffices for FRR entities but not for self-supply LSEs participating in RPM. Because the

resulting curtailment exposure can attach to load supported by an adequate portfolio, the

Commission should reject the resource-specific attribution requirement or require PJM to accept

a portfolio-sufficiency demonstration as an alternative.

           Transferability. PJM misstates EKPC’s concern regarding the lack of transferability of

BYONC by characterizing EKPC’s concern as a request for a liquid secondary market in BYONC.9

EKPC’s concern is narrower. PJM has not justified a rule that permanently strands unused UCAP

MW when load does not materialize as initially forecast or when an LSE’s portfolio needs change.

PJM permits a New Large Load to oversize BYONC for anticipated future growth,10 but prohibits




7
    PJM Answer at 38–39.
8
    See Montalvo Affidavit at PP 28–35; Tucker Affidavit at PP 12, 17–18.
9
    PJM Answer at 39.
10
     Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VII(h).



                                                          5
 unused UCAP MW from being reassigned if that growth does not occur.11 Given that PJM defines

BYONC as UCAP MW and already permits a physical resource to support multiple BYONC

arrangements, this absolute restriction on transferability is not necessary to prevent double-

counting. Verified reporting through the Large Load Registry can preserve the one-MW/one-offset

rule without penalizing prudent forward procurement. The Commission should therefore require

PJM to permit reasonable reassignment of unused BYONC UCAP MW subject to validation and

anti-double-counting safeguards.

           Large Load Definition. PJM’s Answer does not satisfy its burden of proof to justify

applying the extraordinary IRAS curtailment and compensation framework to every qualifying

form of commercial and industrial load growth.12 A Kentucky manufacturing facility below 50

MW today may become subject to IRAS when incremental growth causes the site to exceed 50

MW, even though the LSE has long served the existing facility and planned for ordinary industrial

expansion through its integrated portfolio.13 PJM responds only that its 50 MW threshold follows

Commission guidance and that EKPC showed no basis to distinguish computational load from

other industrial load.14 PJM itself grounds IRAS principally in the speed, concentration, and scale

of data-center growth.15 It has not shown that ordinary manufacturing or industrial expansion

presents the same timing, concentration, or operational risks, or that subjecting such growth to the

12

and this attempt should be rejected. See PJM Answer at 16 (entities protesting the proposed definitions “have shown
no basis for deviating from the Commission’s approach of treating data center or computational, manufacturing,
industrial, or other types of Large Load the same.”).
13
     See EKPC Protest at 25–27; Montalvo Affidavit at P 32.
14
     PJM Answer at 14–16.

Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability,” at 13-14, 21-24 (filed
Aug. 13, 2026).



                                                          6
 same curtailment regime is narrowly tailored to the asserted reliability need.16 The Commission

should require PJM either to narrow the definitions or to establish objective criteria demonstrating

that non-computational load presents the same IRAS-relevant risks.

           Non-IRAS Load May be Subject to Curtailment. Although PJM responds to EKPC’s

BYONC and FRR arguments, it neither cites the Montalvo Affidavit nor answers his showing,

from an operational perspective, that an IRAS instruction may exceed the IRAS-eligible load then

online and available for curtailment. PJM will calculate annual zonal IRAS availability from

registered peak-load quantities and then issue an IRAS Action as a NERC Operating Instruction

to the Electric Distributor. PJM’s IRAS Proposal does not require PJM to limit a real-time directive

to the amount of Eligible New Large Load then online and capable of being curtailed, nor does it

specify whether compliance will be measured by curtailment of IRAS-eligible load or by aggregate

zonal load reduction. That ambiguity matters because a Reliability Coordinator’s Operating

Instruction carries mandatory compliance consequences unless it cannot be physically

implemented or would violate safety, equipment, regulatory, or statutory requirements. An Electric

Distributor should not be forced to choose between noncompliance and curtailing firm customers

outside the IRAS class. The Commission should therefore condition acceptance on inclusion of

the tariff language set out below.17

           Compensation. PJM’s Answer assumes the conclusion EKPC disputes: that IRAS

curtailment is a compensable wholesale service rather than a condition attached to taking service

without recognized capacity support. If IRAS is justified because a New Large Load has not

secured qualifying capacity, PJM must explain why interruption of that load constitutes a service


16
   See Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,196, PP 84–87 (2026) (accepting differentiated treatment where narrowly
tailored to the specific and unique characteristics of high-impact large loads).
17
     See NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108, 114–16 (D.C. Cir. 2017).



                                                        7
 sold to the system rather than the consequence of conditional access. It does not. EKPC’s analogy

to non-firm transmission service remains instructive because interruption is an inherent

characteristic of service taken without the facilities or commitments necessary to support firm

treatment, not a separately compensable product. PJM’s reliance on compensation and

nonperformance rates for committed Demand Resources is inapposite because those resources

assume an RPM capacity obligation, whereas an IRAS-exposed load has not. Nor has PJM

identified the seller, buyer, measurable performance obligation, settlement quantity, or avoided

wholesale cost associated with the asserted service. The proposed default rate may also weaken

the incentive to secure qualifying capacity and, by charging other load in the zone, shift costs to

customers that did not cause the underlying resource adequacy concern. Nor does PJM’s retail-

level waiver option cure the federal default rate or Kentucky’s retained authority over load-

management programs.18 PJM therefore has not shown that the proposed payment reflects a

distinct wholesale service or that allocating its cost to other zonal load follows cost causation.

EKPC requests that the Commission reject Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section X or, at minimum,

sever that provision for a separate section 205 filing supported by an evidentiary record.

        PJM’s September 3 planning-parameter report exposes a separate defect in the proposed

compensation formula. Attachment DD-4, section X(a), sets the default IRAS rate at 50 percent of

the Non-Performance Charge Rate in Attachment DD, section 10A(e). Section 10A(e), however,

calculates that rate using Net CONE for the applicable Locational Deliverability Area (“LDA”)

and Delivery Year, while section X does not identify the LDA applicable to an Eligible New Large

Load. If PJM intends to use the LDA in which the curtailed load is located, the 2029/2030

management programs involving retail loads as a condition of integration of the Kentucky utilities that are members

and Public Service Commission approval).



                                                        8
 parameters imply a default rate of approximately $156/MWh in DOM and $3,109/MWh in

COMED—a twenty-fold difference. That spread is driven by LDA-specific Net CONE, including

forward E&AS offsets, rather than by any stated difference in the IRAS obligation or measured

curtailment. If PJM intends another locational mapping, the tariff does not state it. Either way, PJM

has not explained how the imported capacity-performance benchmark produces a just and

reasonable rate for IRAS.

          Applicability of IRAS to FRR Entities. PJM responds that FRR entities are not similarly

situated to RPM LSEs because an FRR entity must provide capacity for all load in its service area

and may incur an insufficiency charge.20 Even if FRR and RPM are distinct administrative

frameworks, that does not justify an unconditional IRAS exemption where PJM’s premise for the

exemption is that the FRR entity has provided adequate capacity support. Proposed Tariff,

Attachment DD-4, section V(a), excludes New Large Load in an FRR Service Area without

conditioning the exclusion on the sufficiency of the applicable FRR Capacity Plan. PJM’s Answer

therefore does not explain why IRAS should never apply when the FRR Entity’s plan is

insufficient. The relevant distinction is not FRR versus RPM in the abstract; it is whether the load

is supported by sufficient capacity.21 A portfolio-based demonstration cannot be sufficient for FRR

load while an equivalently adequate self-supply portfolio receives no recognition under RPM. The

Commission should require PJM to condition the FRR exclusion on a sufficient FRR Capacity

Plan and to provide a comparable portfolio-sufficiency pathway for self-supply LSEs.




20
     PJM Answer at 61–63.
21
  See also Montalvo Affidavit at PP 36–41. For the first two Delivery Years in which IRAS is proposed to be in effect,
there is no applicable FRR Plan insufficiency charge. See PJM RAA, Schedule 8.1-D FRR Capacity Plans (“Delivery
Years between the 2025/2026 Delivery Year through the 2028/2029 Delivery Year, no FRR Commitment Insufficiency
Charge shall be assessed.”).



                                                         10
            PJM also fails to cure the ambiguity and overbreadth in proposed RAA, Schedule 8.1,

section D.1.1, which would prohibit an FRR Entity from including Existing Generation Capacity

Resources above the amount owned or contracted before June 1, 2027, to serve New Large Load.22

EKPC supports preventing an FRR Entity from withdrawing existing capacity from RPM to serve

new load while the region is short, but the filed language is not limited to Delivery Years in which

IRAS applies or a regional shortfall exists. A permanent restriction untethered to the condition that

purportedly justifies it can foreclose cost-effective capacity and disadvantage future FRR elections

after the asserted emergency has passed.23 The Commission must judge PJM’s filed rate as

proposed and may not supply a narrowing construction that the tariff does not contain. 24 The

Commission should reject the restriction or require PJM to limit it to Delivery Years in which the

relevant IRAS shortfall condition exists.

                   B.       Targeted Tariff Revisions.

           To provide the Commission with administrable relief that preserves the basic structure of

PJM’s filing, EKPC proposes the following limited revisions to address the immediate operational

risk without changing IRAS’s basic structure. The Commission should require PJM to address any

necessary implementation and compliance procedures in a compliance filing.

           Limitation on Interim Resource Adequacy Service Actions. Notwithstanding any other

provision of Attachment DD-4, an Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action directed to an

Electric Distributor shall not exceed the quantity of Eligible25 New Large Load within the


22
     PJM Answer at 61–63.
23
     See EKPC Protest at 35–36.

if its proposed modifications accepted by the utility “involved the Commission’s own original notion of a new form
of rate.”).

                                                       11
 applicable Zone or other area specified in the directive that, at the time the directive is issued: (i)

is consuming electric energy; (ii) remains subject to Interim Resource Adequacy Service; and (iii)

may be curtailed in a manner consistent with applicable state law and regulatory requirements and

without requiring the Electric Distributor to interrupt or reduce service to load that is not receiving

Interim Resource Adequacy Service. Only a verified reduction in Eligible New Large Load then

subject to Interim Resource Adequacy Service shall count toward compliance. A reduction in load

not then subject to Interim Resource Adequacy Service shall not be required or credited for that

purpose.

       Insufficient Available IRAS Load. If an Electric Distributor determines that the quantity

of Eligible New Large Load available for curtailment is less than the quantity stated in an Interim

Resource Adequacy Service Action, the Electric Distributor shall promptly notify PJM and

implement the directive only to the extent consistent with applicable state law and regulatory

requirements. The Electric Distributor shall not be required to interrupt or reduce service to native

load or other load that is not receiving Interim Resource Adequacy Service to satisfy the difference.

An Electric Distributor’s inability to provide the remaining reduction because Eligible New Large

Load is unavailable or because curtailment would conflict with applicable state law or regulatory

requirements shall not constitute noncompliance with the IRAS Action or any NERC Operating

Instruction through which PJM communicates that Action.

               C.      PJM Has Not Carried Its Affirmative Burden Under FPA Section 205.

       EKPC’s Protest raised serious questions concerning the justness and reasonableness of the

IRAS Proposal, and PJM’s Answer does not cure the identified defects. Section 205 places the

burden on PJM to establish that the rates, terms, and conditions it filed are just and reasonable and




                                                  12
 not unduly discriminatory or preferential.26 Although the Commission may accept one of multiple

just and reasonable approaches, it may do so only on the basis of the proposal and evidentiary

record before it.27 It may not presume answers PJM did not provide or rely on post hoc reasoning

to fill material gaps.28 Nor may PJM’s consent to modification supply a substitute design where

the filed proposal lacks support for foundational elements.29 PJM has not supplied a reasoned

record basis for the disputed provisions identified above. EKPC requests that the Commission

reject those provisions or condition acceptance on the specific, limited relief requested above.

           III.      CONCLUSION

           For the foregoing reasons and those set out in EKPC’s Protest and supporting affidavits,

EKPC respectfully requests that the Commission accept this Answer and take such actions as set

forth therein and herein. Specifically, the Commission should reject the proposed compensation

provision and any interpretation that would permit curtailment of non-IRAS load. If the

Commission otherwise accepts IRAS, it should condition acceptance on tariff revisions that

recognize an adequate self-supply portfolio; provide interim recognition to operating resources

pending their first available RPM commitment; permit reasonable reassignment of unused

BYONC UCAP MW subject to verification and anti-double-counting safeguards; limit resource-

to-load attribution where an LSE demonstrates aggregate portfolio adequacy; require objective

criteria before applying IRAS to non-computational load; condition the FRR exemption on a

sufficient FRR Capacity Plan; and limit the FRR resource restriction to the period in which the
